pros: Proven O(V log V) worst-case complexity (unlike Louvain)
Empirically faster than Louvain despite extra refinement phase
Achieves higher or equal modularity scores than Louvain
More stable: reduced sensitivity to random node ordering
Better initialization for each level via refinement
Refinement phase can be customized with different quality functions
Maintains all advantages of Louvain (speed, scalability, hierarchy)
Fewer levels needed for convergence than Louvain
Community structure is more interpretable and reliable
cons: More complex implementation than Louvain (three phases vs two)
Non-deterministic results (same as Louvain, though more stable)
Modularity resolution limit still applies (cannot detect tiny communities)
Cannot detect overlapping communities (hard partitions only)
No theoretical guarantee of global optimality (still heuristic)
Requires careful implementation of connectivity checks
Less widely available in standard libraries than Louvain
May be overkill for very small graphs (< 1000 nodes)
Memory overhead for maintaining refined partition structure
Refinement can split communities into very small pieces in some cases
